comparison: Both evaluate claims C24-C28 regarding erythropoiesis and the mouse model. OpenEval finds the evidence well-supported with statistical significance. Peer reviewers also accept these findings as a core strength of the study, with the editor explicitly acknowledging increased erythropoiesis and Reviewer 1 noting the mouse model as a main strength.

Both address claims C29-C32 about splenomegaly and biphasic response. OpenEval finds the morphological data well-supported though notes mechanism requires further investigation. Peer reviewers accept the splenomegaly finding (editor explicitly states 'increased mature erythrocyte retention in the spleen'), with no challenges to morphological observations.

Both evaluate claims C33-C36 regarding splenectomy experiments. OpenEval finds strong evidence for the spleen's role under hypoxic stress. Peer reviewers are uncertain, with Reviewer 1 stating the 'moderate if not marginal difference' argues against a significant splenic role, and Reviewer 2 noting conclusions sound 'overstated' with only 'very mild' biological increases.

Both address claims C37-C49 about RPM reduction. OpenEval finds strong support from multiple independent methods (flow cytometry, scRNA-seq, immunofluorescence). Peer reviewers express uncertainty, with Reviewer 2 raising significant concerns about data presentation: scRNA-seq graphics are 'very difficult to understand,' clusters not properly labeled, and potential axis mislabeling in Figure 3G.

Both evaluate claims C50-C53 on impaired RBC clearance. OpenEval finds elegant labeling experiments with appropriate methodology and well-justified conclusions. Peer reviewers are uncertain, with Reviewer 1 noting 'direct proof for reduced erythrophagocytosis is compromised due to strong spontaneous loss of labelled red blood cells' and Reviewer 2 pointing out missing time '0' data and potential evidence of increased (not decreased) removal in early hypoxia.

Both address claims C54-C57 about RBC retention in spleen. OpenEval finds strong support from multiple complementary techniques showing consistent results. Peer reviewers also support this finding, with the editor explicitly stating the study shows 'increased mature erythrocyte retention in the spleen' and no reviewer challenging the histological evidence.

Both evaluate claims C58-C63 regarding Tuftsin experiments. OpenEval finds support for causal role of RPM dysfunction, though notes incomplete rescue suggests additional mechanisms. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, with Reviewer 2 stating the experiments are 'not very easy to follow' and questioning what major point the authors wanted to make, indicating unclear logic and interpretation.

Both address claims C64-C72 about ferroptosis markers. OpenEval finds comprehensive molecular support from multiple methods, though notes absence of mitochondrial shrinkage raises questions. Peer reviewers are uncertain, with Reviewer 2 critically noting that markers don't address individual cell types (drops in HO1/FT may be due to RPM depletion rather than ferroptosis), and PBMC data are only 'very loosely linked' to splenic phenotypes.

Both evaluate claims C73-C82 on in vitro ferroptosis experiments. OpenEval finds strong support from primary splenic macrophages with Fer-1 rescue experiments demonstrating causality and mechanistic validation. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, with Reviewer 2 questioning cellular identity and requesting purity data for primary cultures, stating only ensuring these are macrophages could link ferroptosis to RPMs.

Both address claims C8, C110-C111 regarding the overall mechanistic model. OpenEval rates as uncertain, noting individual components are well-supported but the causal chain remains speculative and requires validation in HAPC patients. Peer reviewers also uncertain, with editor stating work 'only incompletely supports the authors' hypotheses' and Reviewer 1 suggesting 'the scientific community should decide whether it is all in all conclusive.'

Both address claim C109 about absence of mitochondrial shrinkage. OpenEval acknowledges this as an appropriate limitation that raises questions about classical ferroptosis. Peer reviewers support this negative finding without challenge, though it raises questions about completeness of the ferroptosis phenotype.

Partial overlap on claim C34 (splenectomy effects). OpenEval R3 finds splenectomy data well-supported. Peer R11 specifically questions this finding with reviewer characterizing authors' response as 'hand waiving,' indicating the significance and explanation remain unclear.

Minimal overlap on claim C25 (routine blood tests). OpenEval R1 finds blood test data well-supported. Peer R11 questions related findings about blood parameters, with reviewer noting unclear significance.
